blocks.content: The story starts with a query that worked perfectly in development.

You're building a social media platform. You write SELECT * FROM posts ORDER BY created_at DESC. It runs in 2ms. You ship it. Users start joining. The posts table grows to 50 million rows. The same query now takes 45 seconds, transfers 8 gigabytes of data, and crashes the client trying to parse it.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785275745688-324560975.png
blocks.alt: A query that runs in milliseconds during development times out once the table reaches tens of millions of rows

blocks.content: You fix it with LIMIT 20. Now the query is fast. But your mobile client needs to show more posts when the user scrolls down. How does it ask for the next 20? And if someone posted something new between the first and second page, does the user see it twice, or miss it entirely?
Then a product manager asks: "Can we add a filter so users can see only posts from people they follow, within the last 7 days, with more than 10 likes, sorted by engagement?"

These are the two problems this topic is about. Pagination is how you break large result sets into manageable chunks. Filtering is how you let clients specify which subset of data they need. Together they're one of the most underestimated surfaces of API design and one of the places where bad decisions compound expensively over time.
1. Why both matter together

Pagination without filtering: you return 20 items per page from a table with 50 million rows. Getting to page 2,500,000 takes 30 seconds. The client can't find what it needs without scrolling forever.

Filtering without pagination: you add WHERE category = 'news' and there are 3 million news posts. You return all 3 million in one response. The server runs out of memory. The network transfer takes minutes.
They compose: filter the dataset to a manageable subset, then paginate through that subset. Done well, every page fetch is fast. Done badly, both problems survive.
2. Pagination: the three strategies
Fetch the next page by skipping a fixed number of rows and returning the following records.
Strategy 1: Offset pagination
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028050-286239461.png
blocks.alt: Offset pagination skips a fixed number of rows before returning the next page

blocks.content: Offset pagination is the oldest and simplest pagination technique.
The idea is straightforward: skip a certain number of rows and return the next set of rows.
This query means, "Skip the first 400 rows and return the next 20 rows." If each page contains 20 items, this is equivalent to requesting page 21.
1. API:

GET /posts?page=21&per_page=20

GET /posts?offset=400&limit=20

blocks.content: <hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">
blocks.text: <hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">

blocks.content: 2. What works well

Offset pagination is easy to understand and implement. Users can directly jump to any page number, such as page 10 or page 500, without visiting the previous pages first. It also works nicely with page navigation like "Page 1 of 2,400" because the system can easily calculate page numbers.
3. What breaks

The database cannot directly jump to row 401. To execute OFFSET 400, it still scans the first 400 rows, discards them, and then returns the next 20 rows. As the offset grows, the query becomes slower.
For example:
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 1000000
blocks.code: LIMIT 20 OFFSET 1000000

codes.javascript: LIMIT 20 OFFSET 1000000
codes.python: LIMIT 20 OFFSET 1000000
codes.java: LIMIT 20 OFFSET 1000000

blocks.content: The database scans and discards one million rows before returning only 20 rows. Deep pages become extremely expensive.

Another problem is data drift. Suppose a user opens page 1 and, before opening page 2, a new row is inserted at the top. All subsequent rows shift by one position. The user may see a duplicate row on page 2 or completely miss a row.
This makes offset pagination unsuitable for frequently changing datasets.

When to use: Offset pagination works well for admin dashboards, reports, and search results where users want page numbers and data does not change frequently. It should generally be avoided for infinite scrolling feeds, social media timelines, and very large datasets with frequent inserts and updates.
Strategy 2: Cursor Pagination (Keyset Pagination)
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785275749274-96847752.png
blocks.alt: Cursor pagination remembers the last item and fetches forward from it, never skipping rows

blocks.content: Cursor pagination does not skip rows like offset pagination. Instead, it remembers the position of the last item returned and fetches the next set of records starting from that point. The database query becomes "give me the next 20 rows after this cursor."

ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

blocks.content: The database does not scan and discard old rows. It uses an index to jump directly to the cursor position. Because of this, page 5,000,000 is almost as fast as page 1. Performance remains consistent even on datasets containing millions of rows.
Another major advantage is stability. If new posts are inserted while the user is scrolling, pages do not shift. Users do not see duplicate records or miss any records.

blocks.content: 3. What works well

Cursor pagination is extremely efficient for large datasets because every request performs an index seek instead of scanning millions of rows. It also works perfectly for continuously changing data because new inserts do not affect the results that the user has already seen.

Cursor pagination does not support random page access. A user cannot directly jump to page 500 because the system needs the cursor from page 499 first. It also does not work well with page-number navigation like "Page 42 of 500."
Another requirement is that the cursor column must be indexed and sortable. If multiple rows can have the same cursor value, additional handling is required.

blocks.content: 5. Cursor implementation: Handling duplicate values
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785275750936-907684617.png
blocks.alt: Using only a timestamp as the cursor breaks down the moment two rows share the exact same value

blocks.content: A common mistake is using only created_at as the cursor. Multiple posts may have exactly the same timestamp, which can lead to duplicate or missing records.
The solution is to use a composite cursor:

SELECT *
FROM posts
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2024-01-15 10:23:45', 'post-123')
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;

SELECT *
FROM posts
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2024-01-15 10:23:45', 'post-123')
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;

FROM posts
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2024-01-15 10:23:45', 'post-123')
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;

blocks.content: The cursor now contains both created_at and id, guaranteeing unique ordering.

When to use: Cursor pagination is the preferred choice for infinite scrolling feeds, social media timelines, chat applications, notification feeds, and any large dataset that changes frequently. It should generally be avoided when users need page numbers or need to jump directly to a specific page.
Strategy 3: Seek Method (Page Tokens)
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028050-442011936.png
blocks.alt: The seek method hands the client an opaque page token that resumes exactly where the last response left off

blocks.content: The seek method is commonly used by search engines such as Elasticsearch, Solr, and Algolia. Instead of using page numbers or offsets, the server returns a page token with the first response. The client sends this token back to fetch the next page of results.

blocks.content: The page token usually contains the sort values of the last document returned and is opaque to the client.
1. Why it matters

Search engines cannot efficiently support deep pagination using OFFSET. A query like page 10,000 would require scanning and sorting millions of documents. Page tokens allow the search engine to continue from the last result directly, making pagination fast and scalable.
2. What works well

Performance remains consistent even for deep pages because the search engine does not need to re-scan earlier results. It also works well with distributed search systems where results come from multiple shards.
3. What breaks
There is no random page access. Users cannot jump directly to page 500 because they need the token from page 499 first.
Page tokens are also tied to a particular search result and sorting order. If the search query changes, the old token becomes invalid.
When to use: The seek method is ideal for search engines, full-text search, log analytics, and document search systems built on Elasticsearch, Solr, or Algolia.
For normal database-backed APIs, cursor pagination is usually the simpler and preferred approach.
3. Filtering: designing the query interface
Filtering lets clients express "which subset of data do I want?" The design question is: how do you express complex filter logic in an HTTP API without reinventing SQL?
1. Simple Field-Based Filtering
Filtering allows clients to request only the records they are interested in by adding conditions to the URL.

4. Complex Filtering
Complex filtering is used when simple query parameters are not enough to express the required conditions.

blocks.content: This approach supports complex conditions such as OR logic, nested filters, and multiple combinations that are difficult to represent in a URL. It is commonly used in search systems, analytics platforms, and reporting APIs.
If your filtering requirements are this complex, consider GraphQL (which makes arbitrary filter expressions natural) or OData
(which has a standardised filter syntax: $filter=(category eq 'tech' or likes gt 1000) and author_id in (1,2,3)).
For most REST APIs, the point where filter complexity exceeds what query parameters handle cleanly is the signal to accept a POST body with a filter object, or to evaluate GraphQL.
4. Database indexing: Where pagination and filtering actually live

WHERE author_id = 123
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

blocks.content: All required data already exists inside the index. The database can answer the query by reading only the index and never touching the main table, making the query even faster.
5. Common mistakes and how to avoid them
blocks.text: 5. Common mistakes and how to avoid them

blocks.content:
["Allowing arbitrary offsets without limits. A client requests OFFSET 50000000 LIMIT 20. Your database tries to scan 50 million rows. Set a maximum offset (e.g., 10,000) and return an error beyond that, with a message suggesting filters to narrow the result set.
","No default ordering. SELECT * FROM posts LIMIT 20 with no ORDER BY returns rows in arbitrary order often primary key order, but not guaranteed by SQL. Pagination is undefined without a deterministic sort. Always specify an order.
","Trusting client-provided sort fields without whitelisting. GET /posts?sort=password_hash or GET /posts?sort=1;DROP TABLE posts--. Always validate sort field names against an explicit whitelist.
","Returning too many fields by default. Returning all 50 columns including large text blobs on a list endpoint is wasteful. Have explicit list and detail views, or support sparse fieldsets.
","The N+1 query in filtering. The filter returns 20 posts. Then you make 20 separate queries to fetch each post's author. Always JOIN or batch-fetch related data.
","Not including the cursor in the API response. Clients need the next_cursor from the server they should not construct it themselves. The cursor format is an internal detail. Encode it opaquely (base64 JSON) so you can change the implementation without breaking clients.
"]

No default ordering. SELECT * FROM posts LIMIT 20 with no ORDER BY returns rows in arbitrary order often primary key order, but not guaranteed by SQL. Pagination is undefined without a deterministic sort. Always specify an order.
Trusting client-provided sort fields without whitelisting. GET /posts?sort=password_hash or GET /posts?sort=1;DROP TABLE posts--. Always validate sort field names against an explicit whitelist.
Returning too many fields by default. Returning all 50 columns including large text blobs on a list endpoint is wasteful. Have explicit list and detail views, or support sparse fieldsets.
The N+1 query in filtering. The filter returns 20 posts. Then you make 20 separate queries to fetch each post's author. Always JOIN or batch-fetch related data.

Not including the cursor in the API response. Clients need the next_cursor from the server they should not construct it themselves. The cursor format is an internal detail. Encode it opaquely (base64 JSON) so you can change the implementation without breaking clients.

7. HLD interview How to talk about this
blocks.text: 7. HLD interview How to talk about this

blocks.content: When designing a social media feed, search API, or any data-heavy system, pagination and filtering should come up naturally.

["Name the choice and justify it. \"For the user's home feed infinite scroll through posts from followed accounts I'd use cursor pagination. Offset pagination has two problems here: performance degrades at depth (users who scroll a lot hit slow pages), and new posts cause duplicates or gaps as the user scrolls. Cursor pagination anchors to a specific position in the dataset and is O(log n) at any depth.\"
","Show you know when to use offset. \"For the admin dashboard showing all orders, I'd use offset pagination with page numbers. Admins want to jump to page 50 to find an order from last Tuesday. The dataset is smaller, admins rarely go past page 100, and they need the total count to know how many orders are in the system.\"
","Address filtering and indexing together. \"The filter combinations drive the index design. If users frequently filter by author, status, and sort by time which is the most common feed query I'd create a composite index on (author_id, status, created_at DESC). Without that index, every feed load is a full table scan on a 50-million-row table.\"
","Mention the total count problem. \"Cursor pagination doesn't naturally support total count you'd need a separate COUNT() which is expensive on large filtered datasets. For the feed, I'd omit total count entirely and just return has_more. For the search results page where users expect '1,234 results found,' I'd either accept the COUNT() cost with caching, or use an approximate count from the search engine.\"
","Handle the edge cases. \"Two things to get right: the cursor must be a composite of sort value + ID to handle ties in the sort column. And filters must be validated against a whitelist before hitting the database you can't let arbitrary client-supplied field names reach your SQL.\"
"]
items: Name the choice and justify it. "For the user's home feed infinite scroll through posts from followed accounts I'd use cursor pagination. Offset pagination has two problems here: performance degrades at depth (users who scroll a lot hit slow pages), and new posts cause duplicates or gaps as the user scrolls. Cursor pagination anchors to a specific position in the dataset and is O(log n) at any depth."

Show you know when to use offset. "For the admin dashboard showing all orders, I'd use offset pagination with page numbers. Admins want to jump to page 50 to find an order from last Tuesday. The dataset is smaller, admins rarely go past page 100, and they need the total count to know how many orders are in the system."

Address filtering and indexing together. "The filter combinations drive the index design. If users frequently filter by author, status, and sort by time which is the most common feed query I'd create a composite index on (author_id, status, created_at DESC). Without that index, every feed load is a full table scan on a 50-million-row table."

Mention the total count problem. "Cursor pagination doesn't naturally support total count you'd need a separate COUNT() which is expensive on large filtered datasets. For the feed, I'd omit total count entirely and just return has_more. For the search results page where users expect '1,234 results found,' I'd either accept the COUNT() cost with caching, or use an approximate count from the search engine."

Handle the edge cases. "Two things to get right: the cursor must be a composite of sort value + ID to handle ties in the sort column. And filters must be validated against a whitelist before hitting the database you can't let arbitrary client-supplied field names reach your SQL."

blocks.content: The depth that separates strong answers: knowing not just which strategy to use, but why the other strategies fail for the specific use case, and how the database layer (indexing, query planning) determines whether the strategy actually performs in production.
